text: Lesson 12 built a flow where Medium and High risk Normal changes route to a CAB-approval stage. It's tempting to read that as just another approval record. The Change Advisory Board is actually a real, recurring review body — stakeholders who look at upcoming changes together before they go live. The flow records that body's decision; it doesn't replace the review.

A real CAB needs to see what's scheduled, together, in one place, and that's what the Change Calendar provides — a visual, calendar-style view of scheduled changes across the instance, filterable by assignment group, CI, or risk. It's what lets the board see overlapping changes and maintenance windows at a glance, instead of reading through tickets one at a time.

The other real capability supporting CAB review is Conflict Detection. When a new change is scheduled, it checks whether the planned window overlaps with another scheduled change affecting the same Configuration Item. If it does, the platform flags a real scheduling conflict directly on the record — surfacing exactly the risk a CAB exists to catch, automatically, before the board even convenes.

A well-implemented instance treats a flagged conflict as something the CAB must explicitly resolve — reschedule one of the changes, or document why running them concurrently is actually acceptable — rather than something that gets silently approved anyway.

Put together: risk from Lesson 11 decides whether CAB review is required, the approval chain from Lesson 12 routes the change there, and the Change Calendar plus Conflict Detection give the board something real to review when it meets. Every piece is doing real work.

A common implementation gap is building the approval flow correctly but never configuring the calendar or conflict detection, leaving the CAB meeting as an unsupported read-through of tickets — the flow works, but the real review stays unsupported. Next up: a full worked lab pulling Lessons 10 through 13 together on one real scenario.
